title: Drafting a Manuscript
answer: Drafting a manuscript is the stage of research where findings, methods, and context are assembled into a structured document for peer review. It covers the title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, and references, along with figures and tables. This work sits inside academic writing and peer review, and it is distinct from data collection, analysis, and the final submission system. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Drafting runs on a mix of writing software, reference managers, and collaboration platforms. Common tools include Microsoft Word, Google Docs, LaTeX, and Overleaf, with Zotero, Mendeley, or EndNote handling citations. Version control, such as Git, and cloud storage help manage drafts across co-authors. Journal submission systems, preprint servers like arXiv, and institutional repositories form the delivery infrastructure. The main work happens in the writing environment, where templates and style guides shape the final document.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done iteratively, starting with an outline and then drafting each section in order or by priority. Authors write, revise, and circulate drafts to co-authors for feedback, often using tracked changes and comments. They follow the target journal's author guidelines for length, formatting, and reference style. Reference managers insert citations and build the bibliography, while plagiarism checks and grammar tools catch issues before submission. A cover letter and suggested reviewers are typically prepared alongside the manuscript.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in drafting center on authorship, originality, and provenance. Authors must agree on order and contributions, avoid plagiarism and duplicate submission, and disclose conflicts of interest. Copyright transfer or open licensing is handled at submission, and preprint policies vary by journal. Provenance means citing the original paper rather than a secondary summary, and this site links to original papers rather than the Consensus search tool. Fabrication, falsification, and image manipulation are serious risks that can lead to retraction.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Drafting is moving toward more AI-assisted writing, with language models used for polishing, outlining, and reference formatting. Journals and conferences are updating authorship policies to address AI contributions, and some require disclosure of AI use. Open peer review, preprints, and registered reports are changing when and how drafts become public. Structured writing and machine-readable metadata may make manuscripts easier to check for reproducibility. The field continues to debate how much AI assistance is acceptable in the drafting process.
